title: Kafka internals
subtitle: Kafka is a set of logs on disk, copied between brokers. Learn which settings decide what is safe, what is ordered, and what pauses.

c.v: In September 2013, Kyle Kingsbury tested a pre-release of Kafka 0.8 with his tool, Jepsen. His question was simple: when Kafka says a write is safe, is it?
, or ISR. A write counted as committed once every member of the ISR had it.

He cut the leader off from its followers. They timed out and dropped out of the ISR, so the leader was alone in it. It kept acking writes that existed only on its own disk. The producer was waiting for every in-sync copy, and it still got "ok".

Then the leader lost its claim, and Kafka elected a follower that was far behind. When the old leader came back, its writes conflicted with the new leader's log and were thrown away. Of 987 acked writes, 520 were lost.
He suggested that Kafka should "block and sound an alarm" instead of silently dropping data.
Kafka later changed its default. Since version 0.11.0.0, it waits for an in-sync replica rather than elect one that is behind.
But two settings still decide whether your writes are safe. Most teams never look at them.

If every in-sync replica dies, Kafka must choose. It can wait for one to come back, or elect any replica that returns first, even one that is behind. The second choice keeps the partition up but may lose committed messages.
Even then, a lone last replica that crashes uncleanly can lose committed data.
KIP-966 adds Eligible Leader Replicas to close this gap. They are on by default in new clusters since Kafka 4.1, but not in 4.0.
Each consumer group has a group coordinator on one broker. When a consumer commits offsets, the coordinator writes them to
, a compacted topic that keeps the latest commit per partition.
By default, the consumer commits offsets every 5 seconds in the background.

In the old "eager" protocol, every member gives up all its partitions, then waits for a new assignment. Nobody reads during that pause.
Cooperative rebalancing, from Kafka 2.4, revokes only the partitions that change owner. Everyone else keeps reading.
The newer protocol from KIP-848 is generally available since Kafka 4.0. It is "fully incremental" and the broker computes the assignment.

Kafka keeps order only inside a partition. Same key, same partition, same order. Across partitions there is no order.
That is why the partition count is hard to change for keyed data. Roughly, the default partitioner picks

For a while, one key's events sit in two partitions, and a consumer can read them out of order. Kafka also cannot reduce the number of partitions.
So pick the count for your peak load, with room to grow.

q.v: A topic has 3 replicas and min.insync.replicas=2. Two brokers are down. A producer with acks=all sends a write. What happens?

options.v: The leader stores it and acks, and copies it later.
The write fails with NotEnoughReplicas, so the producer knows it was not stored safely.
Kafka elects a new leader that is behind.

why.v: With acks=all, a write needs at least min.insync.replicas in-sync copies. One is not enough, so Kafka returns an error instead of a weak ack.

q.v: Events for one order must be read in the order they were sent. What do you do?

options.v: Use the order ID as the key, so all its events go to one partition.
Add more partitions, so the events move faster.

why.v: Kafka keeps order only inside a partition. The key hash sends every event of one order to the same partition.

q.v: You grow a keyed topic from 6 to 12 partitions. What changes?

options.v: Nothing. Kafka moves old messages so each key stays in one place.
New messages for a key may go to a different partition than its old messages, so order per key can break.
Kafka shrinks it back once the load drops.

why.v: Kafka does not move existing data. The key-to-partition mapping changes with the count, and Kafka cannot reduce partitions either.

q.v: What does a tombstone do on a compacted topic?

options.v: It marks a key as deleted. After compaction and a delay, the key's older values and then the tombstone itself go away.

why.v: A tombstone is a message with a key and a null value. Compaction keeps the latest value per key, so the delete wins, and the marker is removed after delete.retention.ms.
